HIP Kernel   
Kernel Execution model.   
Function that runs on the GPU and is invoked by the host application.   
Kernel code is executed by many GPU threads concurrently.   
Each threads do identical   
Data parallelism rather than control flow parallelism   
Host Driven control   
Programming model where kernels are launched explicitly by the host application. 

- Predictableand debuggable programs  
- All execution decisions are visible to the developer.   
- Kernel launches, memory transfers and synchronization points are controlled by the host.   
- HIP does not introduce implicit or hidden execution behaviour. 

HIP Kernl programming. 

- C++ friendly model for expressing massive parallelism for modern GPUs.   
- GPUs apply the same operation via lightweight threads across thousands or millions of data elements simultaneously.   
- Parallel execution enables speed ups for scientific, imaging and simulations workloads.   
- Programming model allows splitting work into small independent tasks with minimal coordination.   
- Foundation for more complex optimizations.   
- CPU \-\> Copy data (Host to Device) \-\> GPU(Device) \- Run Kernel / Compute \-\> Copy results (Device \-\> Host) \-\> CPU (Host) \- Validate or Use results. 

Thread Hierarchy: GRID \-\> Block \-\> Threads.   
Grid contains blocks. Block contains a group of threads. Threads within a block execute concurrently on the GPU.   
Identifiers: 

- Runtime assigns identifiers to blocks and threads.   
- Kernels use identifiers to determine which portion of the data to process.   
- Basis for computing global indices and distributing work across the GPU.   
- Bug Source: Incorrect assumptions about block or thread organizations can lead to:   
  Overlapping work or missing data elements or invalid memory access. 

Global indexing:   
Allows each GPU thread to determine exactly which data element to be processed.   
Index Compopnents. 

- Each thread has an index within its block.   
- Each block has an index within the grid.   
- Global Calculations for Unique Thread Mapping. 

1D, 2D, and 3D are all based on this:   
1D: Each GPU thread is mapped ot a single element in a linear array. 

- Follows one thread per element execution approach.   
- Global identifies which array element a thread proceses.   
- Mapping ensures independent execution with no overlap   
- Avoids unintended data access.   
- Linear access patterns are predictable   
- Simpler to debug.

2D: Data is naturally in a spatial form like matrices or images. 

- Threads are mapped to 2 D (x, y) coordinates derived from block and thread identifiers.   
- Allows parallel execution to reflect the logical layout of the data   
- Improves readability and correctness   
- 2D coordinates checks are required along both axes.   
- Invalid memory access at borders are eliminated. 

3D Thread Indexing: 3D is used when data represents a volume as in a scientific simulation or spatial models.   
3 coordinates width, height and depth. 

- Each thread will directly correspond to one element within a 3D data volume.   
- 3D coordinates are linearized for memory access.   
- Safety checks apply to all 3 dimensions and guarding is essential.   
- Safety requirements increase in dimensions.   
- Same defensive pattern is reusd. 

Bounds and Guards: 

- Bounds Valid range of data positions based on input sizes.   
- Challenge: Kernel launches often create more threads than number of data elements.   
- Grid dimensions are often rounded up to simplify launch configuration and ensure data elements.   
- Not all threads map to valid data within the bounds of the input.   
- Extra threads must be handled explicitly.   
- Allowing unrestricted execution leads to incorrect results or program instability. 

Solution: Guards: 

- Ensures correctness and stability.   
- Applies uniformly across dimensions.   
- Checks whether each thread corresponds ot a valid data position within bounds before memory access or computation  
- Applies a defensive pattern to 1D, 2D and 3D index models.   
- Provides safe and predictable GPU execution. 

Common GPU indexing mistakes: 

- Missing or Incorrect Bounds: Invalid memory access or Corrupted output when thread operate outside the valid range.   
- Incorrect Linearization: Threads compute the wrong memory location and access unintended data elements.   
- Off-by-one errors: At data boundaries when grid sizes are rounded up or when handling edge conditions.   
- Configuration issues: Incorrect assumptions about data dimensions or choosing incorrect grid sizes can cause portions of the input to be skipped entirely. 

Kernel launch

- Host CPU: Host application launches hte GPU kernel using the HIP runtime APIs.   
- Grid and Block configuration: Host specifies the grid and block dimensions for thread createion.   
- HIP kernels launch: kernel execution begins asynchronous on the GPU edge  
- GPU thread execution: threads are created based on the grid and block configuration and begin execution at the kernels entry function. 

Block and grid dimensions. 

- How many threads per block hardware limits   
- Portabiliy 

Grid dimensions: 

- Derived from total amount of data that needs to be processed.   
- Large enough to include extra threads to cover all required elements.   
- 

Launch Configuration: Kernel templates:   
Outlines the standard pattern for launching a kernel

- Computations of grid dimensions from the data size and the block size selection that conforms to hardware limits  
- Error checks are performed to catch configuration or runtime errors.   
- Synchronization may be used during development to validate correctness. 

Deterministic and initialization

- Determinisim and Benefits: Deterministic behaviour means a kernel produces the same results with the same inputs.   
- Repeatable results simpi=lify debugging and validation.   
- Non repeatable results hide logical and indexing issues.   
- Established determinism early builds confidence before deeper validation or performance analysis.   
- Uninitialized memory: Uninitialized memory is a common source of non-deterministic behaviour.   
- If input or output buffers are not explicitly initialized, threads may operate on undefined values.   
- Explicitly initialization of inputs and output buffers removes ambiguity and ensures results reflect kernel logic. 

Error checking and Synchronization

- Error detection  
  - Kernel launches fail silently if errors are not checked.   
  - Runtime APIs for querying kernel launch status.   
  - Errors checks recommended immediately after kernel launch.   
- Synchronization usage   
  - Synchronization forces completion of GPU work.   
  - Required for debugging and validating results.   
  - Avoid excessive synchronization- can hide performance issues. 

Validation : GPU vs CPU   
Always validate before optimizing optimizing incorrect code apllifies errors.   
Use GPU references and tolerance based comparisons to establish correctness. 

Host vs Kernel Responsibilities  
Host responsibilities

- Kernel launch configuration  
- Memory management  
- Execution flow orchestration

Kernel responsibility

- Computation only focus   
- Each thread platforms assigned work using provided indices  
- No management of memory moment or execution order. 

Event timing 

- Eventimings are accurate compared to host side times. Intended for performance analysis not for correctness during development.   
- Only after correctness is confirmed.   
- Timing is not  a debugging substitute. 

Debugging checklist for kernel development. 

- Approach incrementally start with small input sizes to make it easier to reason about the thread behaviour.   
- Verify that indexing and boundary conditions are correct.   
- Add error checks and synchronization points to confirm kernel launches and execution complete as expected.   
- Compare GPU results with CPU output side by side to confirm correctness and diagnosis discrepancies.   
- Validate kernels step by step to simplify debugging and build confidene. 

HIP Patterns: 

- SAXPY Pattern: single precision A x X \+ Y  
  - Simple element wise computation: Each thread performs the same arithmetic operation on a different array element.   
  - Natural fit for a 1D indexing model.   
  - Threads compute a global index, apply a bounds guard, then performa  computation on device resident data.   
- 2D Stencil: Used when each output value depencds on a neighborhood of input values.   
  - Each thread computes one output but reads multiple neighboring inputs around its assigned position.   
  - Uses image processing and scientific computations. 

Reduction pattern: Combines many input values into a single output value

- Requires threads to work together rather than independently.   
- Threads compute partial results and combine them via synchronization.   
- Are common in real applications and form the basis for more advanced algorithms.   
- Recognizing when aproblem is reduction helps wih choosing the right strategy. 

HIP Compilation and Toolchain \- Overview 

- HIP Compilation has the following steps   
  - HIP source is parsed \-\> IR \-\> Optimize \-\> GPU code object   
  - 

HIP Toolchain 

- Multistage pipeline that transforms unified HIP source into executable GPU code.   
- Frontend: HIP Source Code  
  - Host and device code (C++ programming)   
- HIP source code(frontend) \-\> Clang and hipcc(frontend) \-\> LLVM IR (backend) \-\> AMD GPU (backend) \-\> GPU BInary Output. .    
- 1\. Host and device code (C++ programming)  
- 2\. Device declaration identification, HIP construct parsing and GPU code preparation.   
- 3\. Architecture-agnostic optimization before backend generates AMDGPU-specific instructions.   
- 4\. HSACO output, an ELF based binary with GPU kernel code and resource metadata.  
- Toolchain embeds code variants to enable applications to run on multiple AMD GPU generations without source changes. 

Why understanding it is required? 

- Host device Separation: Helps issues from incorrect device annotations, unsupported language constructs, or mismatched compile flags.   
- Multi-architecture Workflows: Enables producing binaries that run across diverse GPU cluster/cloud environments.   
- Runtime Loader Behavior: Anticipated startup performance, mitigates HSACO load latency and confirm correct architecture selection at execution.   
- LLVM and Backend Insights: Allows consideration on register pressure, wavefront utilization andmemory coalescing for better performance. 

Host vs Device compilation: 

- Host:   
  - C++ compilation   
  - Linked with HIP runtime libraries   
  - Host process: Kernel launches, memory transfers, and synchronization.   
- Device:   
  - GPU specific compilation   
  - IR transformations   
  - Backend lowering   
  - HSACO generation. 

Compilation Workflow

- Compilation workflow has 2 steps Offline / ahead of time (AOT) Compilation  
  - Ideal for production environments  
  - Performed in two steps:   
  - Step 1: Host code compilation   
    - Code compiled with amdclang++ or hipcc in a single step.   
  - Step 2: Device code compilation:   
    - Code embedded into the host object file.   
  - Runtime / JIT Compilation:   
    - Useful for:   
      - Development environments   
      - Distributing software to systems without knowledge of the GPU.   
      - hiprtc\* API used for runtime compilation. 

Multiple compilation paths exist because modern GPU applicaitons vary when kernel variants are known. 

- Static kernel compilation (AOT): When implementations and usage patterns are known at build time.   
  - AOT compilations leveraged for optimal runtime performance and minimal overhead.   
- Dynamic Kernel Compilations (real time compilation-RTC):   
  - Runtime compilation for dynamic problem sizes or domain specific code generation.   
  - Workloads like FFT, sorting and ML with runtime speacilizations.   
- Hybrid compilation approach  
  - Performance critical kernels are compiled ahead of time.   
  - Speacialized or rare kernels are compiled through hipRTC. 

Ahead of time (AOT) compilation: 

- AOT compiles GPU executable code during build time using tools like hipcc and amdclang++, embedding device images in executables.   
- Working:   
  - Parses the HIP source, separates host and device code. \-\> Compiles host and device with appropriate backend \-\> Embeds compiled device images into the final executable.   
- Advantages of ahead of time compilation   
  - Provides faster startup as kernels are precompiled and ready to run.   
  - Offers performance predictability, build system integration, and early validation.   
- Disadvantages  
  - Struggles with increased build time and binary sizes when targeting multiple GPU architectures or complex kernel variants.   
- Tradeoffs between AOT and RTC.   
  - AOT reduces runtime overhead and increased predictability.   
  - RTC offers flexibility with higher runtime expenses and additional dependency requirements. 

HIP toolchain COmpilation 

- Clang \- amdclang++ enables precise control over frontend behaviour, IR generation and device compilation flags for HIP development.   
  - Architecture Specification   
    - Explicit offload architecture flags for device targeting are required.   
  - Debugging and Experimentation  
    - Experimenting with specific optimization passes, debugging IR-generation issues and analyzing backend transformations.   
    - Ideal for research, profiling and low-level debugging.   
  - Amdclang++ complements hipcc by providing a deeper configuration layer for specialized workflows.   
- Hipcc   
  - Standard high-level compilation entry point for most HIP developers.   
  - Wrapper around Clang adn backend tools to coordinate host and device compilation via a unified command.   
  - Key features   
    - Auto-configures HIP runtime include paths and injects required compiler flags   
    - Determines offload architecture from environment or user input   
    - Supports multi-architecture builds, embedding multiple HSACO variants in single executable.   
  - Benefits:   
    - Abstracts complex Clang/LLVM flags and reduces misconfiguration risk.   
    - Simplifies developer workflows and improves productivity by reducing cognitive overhead.   
- Amdclang++ Device code Identification:   
  - Kernel function identification:   
    - Scan HIP source for functions marked global, device or host device to find GPU \-relevant code.   
  - Device specific AST conversion: Build an AST subtree capturing GPU functions, intrinsic calls and thread hierarchy expressions for device compilation.   
  - Device Comiplation Queue: Queue identified kernel entry points for LLVM transformation and backend lowering to produce device code.   
  - Accurate Semantic Analysis: Use Clang’s HIP integration to ensure precise host/device analysis and avoid misclassification that can cause runtime or linking errors.   
- LLVM IR Generation fro Device Code.   
  - LLVM IR captures GPU logic in SSA form with memory hierarchy, threading models, math operations for device code.   
  - Address space lowering \- Global, local, shared and constant memory are represented in the IR.   
  - Architecture-agnostic \- IR remains target-independent until AMDGPU optimization passes are applied.   
  - Thread and Block Index Intrisics: Thread and block index intrinsics lowered into IR level expressions referencing special registers or built in functions.   
  - Key IR Optimization Passes  
- Key IR Optimization Passes.   
  - LLVM applies numerous optimization passes to prepare HIP device IR for backend lowering.   
  - Common transformations include:   
    - Scalar representation of aggregates (SROA): Breaks structs/small arrays into individual scalar components for efficient register allocation, avoiding unnecessary memory traffic and enabling further optimization on each field independently — critical for register-constrained GPU kernels.  
    - Aggressive inlining: Substitutes called functions directly at their call sites, reducing call overhead in deeply nested GPU kernels (where call/return is costlier than on CPUs) and exposing more code to further optimization.  
    - Constant Propogation: Reduces unnecessary computations by propagations by known constant values.   
    - Loop Optimizations: Exploits GPU ALU throughput (eg.unrolling and vectornization)  
- AMD GPU Backend Compilation:   
  - AMDGPU backend transforms LLVM IR into native ISA for AMD GPUs.   
  - SelectionDAG Lowering: Maps IR instructions to hardware supportable operations  
  - Wavefront Scheduling: Reorders instructions based on dependencies to minimize pipeline stalls and hazards.   
  - Register allocation: Assigns registers to physical SGPRs and VGPRs with architecture constraints  
  - Instruction selection: Fine tune ALU, memory and control flow operations.   
  - Code emission Emits the assembled ISA into HSACO .text section.   
- HSACO Code Object Structure  
  - HSACO is an ELF based binary format containing:   
    - Kernel ISA (.text): .text section stores the kernels assembled instructions   
    - Constants (Read-only storage): .rodata captures immutable constants and lookup tables.   
    - Metadata (.note): .note section contains metadata for  
      - Kernel arguments  
      - Register usage   
      - Implicit parameters   
      - Dispatch requirements.   
      - Alignment rules.    
    - Symbol Tables: provides names entry points that the runtime loader resolves at launch.   
    - Kernel Metadata:   
      - Kernel metadata is HSACO guides the ROCM runtime to prepare dispatch packets for each kernel:   
        - Registers: ENsure SGPR and VGPR counts are available at launch.   
        - Local Data Share (LDS): Enforce hardware limits for LDS usage.   
        - Argument Descriptors: Specify memory offsets, pointer qualifiers and hidden parameters.   
        - Execution Configuration: Encode wavefront configuration and implicit arguments for GPU kernel execution.  
  - HSACO Inspection tools:   
    - Llvm-objdump: Disassembles kernel ISA to inspect low-level instructions and kernel behaviour.   
    - Readelf: Examines ELF headers and sections to view code-object structure and contents.   
    - Metadata Viewers Display SGPR/VGPR/LDS usage to diagnose register pressure and confirm memory-instruction lowering. 

Module 2: Runtime compilation, hipRTC and Multi-Architecture

- Parses the HSACOs ELF sections and reads the metadata for kernel dispatch.   
- Resolves the kernel symbol using the metadata, allowing the application to reference the compiled GPU function   
- Constructs a dispatch packet filing in grid and block sizes, kernel arguments and resource requirements.   
- Submits the dispatch packet to the GPU queue and launches the kernel.   
- Dynamiz data loading:   
  - hipModuleLoad: Enables dynamic loading of kernel modules at runtime for flexible execution.   
  - hipModuleGetFunction: Retrieves kernel functions from loaded modules for execution.  
  - hip ModuleLaunchKernel: Launches kernel functions with the runtime execution pipeline.   
- HIP Runtime Compilation:   
  - hipRTC enables runtime compilatnio of GPU kernels useful for dynamic optimization and application specific tuning, especially when kernel code dependdss on runtime parameters.   
  - Steps   
    - Provide kernel source as strings (embedded text, config files or code generators).   
    - Create a hipRTC program to manage compilation   
    - Compile to a GPU code object then load into HIP modules enabling specialized, performance adaptive workloads.   
- hipRTC Workflows:   
  - Program creation \- Create a hiprtcprogram to encapsulate a compilation session and pass the kernel source strings and optional header text.   
  - Compilation and Logs \- Invoke hiprtcCompileProgram with required flags, then retrieve compiler logs via hiprtcGetProgramLog to diagnose warnings/errors.   
  - Code retrieval: Use hiprtcGetCodeSize/hiprtcGetCode to obtain the HSACO code object and load it into a GPU module with hipModuleLoadData.   
  - Kernel Execution: Extract the kernel handle and execute the kernel with hipModuleLaunchKernel.  
- Runtime Source Requirements and Constraints   
  - Hiprtc requires careful source management because it cannot access filesystem infrastructure at runtime.   
  - A few things to keep in mind:   
    - Explicit header management: Include all headers beyond built in HIP headers manually because hipRTC cannot access filesyste or system include paths.   
    - Self-contained Source Structure: Provide all code needed for compilation as string inputs, ensuring a self contained source without external dependencies.   
    - Kernel name resolution: Ensure kernel names are unmangled or retrievable using hipRTC APIs for correct linking during runtimg compilation  
  - hipRTC Compilation Options.   
    - hipRTC supports a wide range of compilation options similar to hipcc:   
      - Target Architecture Selection: Ensures the generated code object is optimized for the current GPU.   
      - Optimization Levels: Control instruction selection register usage and inlining decisions, influencing kernel runtime performance.   
      - Language Standard configuration: Configures language standards like c++ versions to enable newere programming features in kernels. 

hipRTC runtime Compilation \- Example: 

- HIP provides API functions to compile source code into launchable kernel code.   
- Obtain Source code \-\> Allocate program \-\> Compile program \-\> Get compile kernel / Get compile messages \-\> Launch Kernel \-\> Cleanup.   
- Obtain Source code and allocating a program  
  - Prepare the kernel source: either embed it as a string or generate it at runtime.   
  - Be aware that embedded source strings can be extracted by determined users, if the code must remain secret, avoid runtime compilation.   
- Compile the program:   
  - Compile the program hiprtc hiprtcCompileProgram  
  - Get compiler messages: hiprtsResult hiprtsGetProgramLogSize  
- Get compiled kernel and launch   
  - Compile the kernel: hiprtcResult hiprtcGetCodeSize, hiprtcResult hiprtsGetCode  
  - Launch the kernel: hiperror\_t hipmoduleLaunchKernel  
- Cleanup  
  - hiprtcResult hiprtcDestroyProgram.

TargetIDs and MUltiarch Binaries

- TargetIDs in HIP  
  - Specify AMD GPU architectures and associated features during compilation.   
  - Target IDs

| Target ID | Meaning |  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| gfx90a | CDNA2 |  |
| gfx942 | CDNA3 architecture |  |
| xnack+ | Enable page migration |  |
| sramecc+ | Enable SRAM ECC |  |
|  |  |  |

  - Why they encode?   
    - Microarchitectural modal   
    - Feature toggles that influence code generation and behaviour  
  - Why they matter?   
    - Allows the compiler to generate optimized device code.   
    - Creates multi-target binaries with multiple code object variants.  
- Multi-architecture Builds  
  - Build a single HIP executable containing multiple HSACO variants for different AMD GPU architectures.   
  - Enhances portability across heterogenous clusters.   
  - Ensures efficient execution without rebuilding per GPU model.   
  - Multi-architecture binaries increases size and build time but simplify deployment and long term maintenance.   
- Fat binary structure  
  - Aggregates multiple HSACO code objects into a single executable, each with metadata on its target GPU architecture.   
  - Selects the most appropriate code object. 

Performance Expectations After Porting 

- Functional correctness is not performance parity, correct results can still have different performance.   
- Initial HIP ports typically underperform until retuned, CUDA specific optimizations may not map directly to AMD GPUs.   
- AMD execution width varies ex: RDNA GPU support 32 or 64 lane wavefronts.  
- Register usage (VGPR pressure) can affect occupancy more aggressively.   
- LDS differs from CUDA shared memory in bank structure patterns. 

| CUDA Platform (NVIDIA) | HIP/ROCm Platform (AMD) |
| :---- | :---- |
| GPU computing platform with C/C++ interfaces:  Runtime API \- simplifies use with implicit context handling.  Driver API \- provides explicit contexts, modules and kernel dispatch		 | Open GPU computing platform:  HIP provides a CUDA like C++ runtime API for source level portability.  ROCm toolchain based on LLVM and Clang.  |
| Device code compiled into PTX and architecture specific cubin binaries.  | Device code compiled directly to the AMDGPU ISA and packaged as a hsaco code objects.  |
| Cubin or JIT compiles device code selected for target GPU at runtime. | Appropriate hsaco code object selected for the target GPU at runtime.  |
| Compilation and execution model serves as the baseline for many GPU applications | Compilation and runtime behaviour differ from CUDA and must be considered during migration.  |

- Migration Notes:   
  - Both platforms support math and communication libraries and profiling tools and require explicit host device management and kernel launches.   
  - Core programming abstractions (kernels, threads, and memory spaces) map directly across platforms.   
  - CUDA Driver API usage must be refactored manually for HIP/ROCm platform.   
  - Module loading and context creation should be validated under HIP/ROCm   
  - Device image building strategy (CUDA fatbins vs ROCm hsaco code objects) must be accounted for.   
  - CUDA can JIT compile PTX for forward compatibility, ROCm uses ahead of time AMD GPU ISA objects adn requires explicitly offload targets. 

API Layers: Runtime vs Driver: 

| CUDA Platform | HIP/ROCm Platform  |
| :---- | :---- |
| CUDA provides two public APIs Runtime API Driver API | HIP provides a runtime API modeled after the CUDA runtime API |
| Applications can use either API independently or mix both Runtime and Driver APIs | HIP does not expose a CUDA style driver API lower level ROCm components are abstracted from application code. |

Migration Notes: 

- HIPIFY translates CUDA Runtime API calls, refactor CUDA Driver API usage manually.   
- Avoid mixing CUDA runtime and driver APIs, rely on a consistent runtime interface for portability.   
- Validate module loading and kernel dispatch behaviour after porting.   
- Update CUDA specific error handling to use HIP equivalents for consistent behaviour.   
- Verify no CUDA driver headers remain in the codebase. 

Terminology and API mapping: 

| CUDA Platform | HIP/ROCm platform |
| :---- | :---- |
| Runtime APIs use the cuda\* prefix  | Runtime APIs use the hip\* prefix |
| Common types include cudaError\_t, cudaStream\_t and cudaEvent\_t | Common types include hipError\_t, hipStream\_t, and hipEvent\_t |
| Memory APIs include cudaMalloc, cudaFree and cudaMemcpy | Memory APIs include hipmalloc, hipFree and hipMemcpy |
| Kernel launches use \<\<\<\>\>\> execution syntax | Kernel launches use the same \<\<\<\>\>\> syntax or hipLaunchKernelGGL.  |

Migration Notes: 

- Verify all cuda \* APIs are replaced with hip\* equivalents after HIPIFY.   
- Review struct and handle type differences between CUDA and HIP for compatibility.   
- Check kernel launch arguments to confirm correct preservation during translation.   
- Validate error-handling semantics using the HIP runtime to ensure consistent behaviour.   
- Rechecklocations where hIPIFY inserted TODO (to do) markers for manual interventions. 

Execution Model 

| CUDA Platform | HIP/ROCm Platform |
| :---- | :---- |
| Threads execute in warps of 32 threads | Threads execute in wavefronts of 64 on CDNA architectures and 32/64 on RDNA architectures.  |

- Both use same hierarchical execution model: Grid \-\> Block \-\> Thread; supports 1D, 2D, 3D indexing.   
- Built in variables used, including threadIdx, blockIdx, blockdim, gridDim and warpsize. 

Migration notes: 

- Do not hardcode warpsize, query warpsize for portability.   
- Adapt warp level operations for 32 or 64 lane wavefronts on AMD GPUs.   
- Retune block sizes based on compute unit occupancy for the target architecture.   
- Reassess register usage (VGPR pressure) to avoid limiting parallelism.   
- Adjust shared memory / LDS layouts to align with AMD bank structures and avoid conflicts   
- Reprofile memory access patterns to ensure efficient coalescing on the target hardware.

Memory Model 

| CUDA platform  | HIP/ROCm platform |
| :---- | :---- |
| Unified Virtual Addressing (UVA) and Unified Memory support prefetch and memory advice mechanisms  | Managed and host mapped memory options provie controls and constraints.  |

- Global memory is large and off chip  
- Shared memory (called LDS on AMD) is on chip and scoped to a thread block.   
- Local memory represents per thread storage.   
- Constant and texture/surface memory provide speacialized access paths.   
- Shared / LDS memory is used for tiling and improving data locality.   
- Global memory access should be coalesced and aligned to achieve high bandwidth. 

Migration notes: 

- Retune memory usage patterns to match AMD GPU behaviour.   
- Adjust LDS tile sizes and ensure bankfriendly layouts to avoid conflicts and maximize throughput.   
- Avoid large per thread local arrays to prevent register spilling into global memory.   
- Revalidate global memory access patterns for proper coalescing and alignment.   
- Reevaluate kernel configurations originally tuned for 32 thread warps.   
- Verify managed and host mapped memory usage aligns with ROCm semantics.   
- Validate alignment constraints to prevent unexpected behaviour. 

Memory coherency

- For both cuda platform and hip/rocm platform  
  - Coherence has a cost and should notbe assumed implicitly.  
  - Write visibility may lag during kernel execution,rely on explicit synchronous mechanisms.   
  - Coherence guaranteed at kernel boundaries.   
  - Correctness inside a running kernel depends on using the appropriate synchronization primitives.   
  - Explicit synchronization is used to avoid subtle data races and maintain portability.

Migration notes: 

- Use explicit synchronization (barriers, memory fences, atomics) to ensure memory visibility.   
- Avoid implicit assumptions about intra-kernel coherence, updates may not be immediately visible during kernel execution.   
- Validate cross-block communication using streams and events.   
- Reassess coherence guarantees for managed and host mapped memory under the Rocm model   
- Recheck ordering assumptions made in the original CUDA implementation after migrations. 

Host device interactions: 

- CUDA platform and HIP/ROCm platform both:   
  - Streams enable asynchronous kernel execution and memory operations.   
  - Events used to express dependencies and measure execution timing.   
  - Support for peer access depending on hardware topology.   
  - Graph based APIs that define and execute sequences or operations (features may vary)

Migration notes: 

- Preserve stream ordered execution to maintain correct operation sequencing.   
- Map CUDA streams / events to HIP equivalents(eq. cusa streams\_t \-\> hipStream\_t) and update event types.   
- Replace NVTX profiling markers with roctx for ROCm tool compatibility.   
- Revalidate asynchronous memory copy behaviour on target hardware.   
- Verify peer access support based on system topology and AMD GPU capabilities. 

Module 2: Migration strategies, debugging and validation. 

| CUDA Platform | HIP/ROCm Platform |
| :---- | :---- |
| Nvcc generates PTX and architecture specific cubin binaries | Compiled AMDGPU ISA and hsaco code objects generated via hipcc (Clang-based) |
| PTX and cubins are bundled into fatbins within host executable | Multiple –offload-arch-gfx\* targets can be bundled into a single binary  |
| Driver selects a matching cubin or JIT compiles PTX into native instructions | Runtime selects the appropriate code object for the target GPU. |

Migration Notes: 

- Update build configuration (replace nvcc with hipcc or a Clang based HIP flow)  
- Specify offloads targets with –offload-arch=gfx\*  
- Update include paths and linking configuration for ROCm libraries.   
- Validate that generated hsaco code objects load and execute correctly at runtime.   
- Compare compiler warnings and errors before and after migration to identify compatibility issues or missed translations

Librariy Mapping

| Area  | CUDA API | HIP/ROCm API |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| BLAS | cuBLAS / cuBLASLt | rocBLAS / hipBLAS |
| FFT | cuFFT / cuFFTDx | rocFFT / hipFFT |
| Random Number Generation (RNG) | cuRAND | rocRAND/ hipRAND |
| Sparse Operations | cuSPARSE / cuSPARSELt | rocSPARSE / hipSPARSE / hipSPARSELt |
| Solvers | cuSOLVER | rocSOLVER / hipSOLVER |
| MultiGPU communication | NCCL | RCCL |

Migration Notes

- Choose API strategy   
  - hip\* wrapper APIs for minimal changes and portability.   
  - roc\* libraries for advanced features and improved performance.   
- Validate numerical correctness across CUDA and ROCm library implementations.   
- Verify handle and descriptor compatibility after migration.   
- Benchmark library kernels on AMD GPUs to evaluate performance. 

Unsupported / Different CUDA features

- Some CUDA features lack direct HIP equivalents.   
- Dynamic Parallelism \- kernels launching other kernels on the device must be refactored, typically using host side or alternative execution strategies.   
- Certain CUDA intrinsics may require alternative implementations.   
- Some CUDA libraries may required replacement with HIP wrappers or native ROCm libraries.   
- Tools: hipify-clang reports unsupported or partially supported constructs during translation. 

Common migration pitfalls

- Assuming hard coded warp / wavefront size is 32 (AMD GPUs may use 32 or 64 lane wavefronts)  
- Relying on implicity memory coherence without proper synchronization  
- Expecting immediate performance parity without retuning block sizes, shared / LDS memory usage and memory access patterns.   
- Forgetting to update compiler flags and gfx targets or mixing CUDA and HIP headers or libraries.   
- Skipping validation after replacing libraries can cause subtle numerical errors.  
- Error handling: 

| CUDA Platform | HIP/ROCm Platform |
| :---- | :---- |
| Runtime calls return cuda\_error\_t values | Runtime calls return hipError\_t values |
| cudaGetLastError() and cudaPeekAtLastError() to retrieve launch errors | hipGetLastError() and hipPeekAtLastError() to retrieve launch errors.  |
| cudaGetErrorString() to retrieve error messages | hipGetErrorString() to retrieve erro messages |

Both platforms: 

- Kernel launches are asynchronous (errors may surface later)   
- Errors may require explicit synchronization to surface reliably.

Debugging and Profiling 

| CUDA Platform | HIP/ROCm Platform |
| :---- | :---- |
| Cuda-gdb for source level debugging | Rocdb for source leve debugging |
| Nsight Compute for kernel level metrics and Nsight Systems for system wide timelines | Rocprof (rocprofv2) for kernel level metrics and roctracer for system level tracing |
| NVTX markers for timeline annotation | Roctx markers for timeline annotation. |

Migrations Notes: 

- Insert synchronization points to isolate kernel launch errors and make debugging predictable	  
- Learn Rocm debugging and profiling tools (rocgdb, rocprof and roctracer)   
- Replace CUDA NVTX markers with roctx markers for timeline annotation in ROCm tools.   
- Return kernels after profiling due to different performance characteristics on AMD GPUs. 

Validation strategy after migration (steps)

- Verify functional correctness using unit and integration tests.   
- Validate numerical accuracy and floating point tolerance.   
- Begin performance profiling and optimization   
- Maintain dual builds (CUDA \+ HIP) during transition.   
- Revalidate after compiler, driver or ROCm stack updates. 

Migration checklist

- Run hipif-clang and review the translation logs for unmapped or partially supported constructs  
- Replace CUDA libraries with hip\* wrappers or native roc\* libraries.   
- Refactor device side kernel launch (dynamic parallelism) into host driven or alternative workflows.   
- Audit warp-level code to ensure correct adaption to both 32 and 64 lane wavefront configuration.   
- Update the build system to use hipcc and include the appropriate gfx targets.   
- Profile application, retune occupancy and memory behavior and verify numerical correctness and benchmark performance. 

Triton Programming Model 

- High performance GPU kernels in a  python kinda way. 

Blocks in triton 

- Organizes computation on data blocks   
- One program per block 

Data is organized into blocks similar to how Grids are split into blocks in CUDA.  
Triton primitives

- Primitives inside program to express parallelism   
- Vectorized operations (loading, computing, storing)  
- No explicit management of threads and vectorization.   
- Triton program  
  - Thread id   
  - Single instruction multi data.(SIMD)  
- All operations are vectorized  
- Memory Hierarchy Awareness   
  - Structure your kernel (tile / block) and hand the memory stuff to triton. 

Meta Parameters

- Meta-parameters autotune  
- BLOCK\_SIZE / TILE\_SIZE / NUM\_WARPS   
- Finding the best meta parameters: tune.autotune decorator. 

Tritons programming model naturally integrates with pytorch.   
You can pass it as triton.jit and directly pass arguments.

Summary 

- Triton divides work into programs that handle blocks of data.   
- Inside each program you write vectorized operations using Triton’s API.   
- You must be aware of memory access patterns to reach peak performance.   
- You can tune meta-parameters for efficience, often with the help of autotuning.   
- Triton integrates smoothly with PyTorch, so you don’t need to step out of your deep learning workflow. 

Vector Add Kernel From Real-life 

- Ubiquitous in AI workloads   
  - Bias addition, weight updates, residual connection   
- Simple yet powerful   
  - Focus on programming model, not complex math.   
- Foundation for advanced kernels programming   
  - Matrix multiplication, reductions, etc. 

Writing triton kernels   
Vector addition \- Naive 

```py
@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, 
		y_ptr, 
		output_ptr, 
		n_elements, 
		BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr, 
		):
pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE 
offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
mask = offsets < n_elements 
x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
output = x + y 
tl.score(output_ptr + offsets, output, mask = mask)

```

```py
def add(x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor): 
	output = torch.empty_like(x)
assert x.device == y.device and output.device == y.device 
	n_elements = output.numel()
	grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(n_elements, meta['BLOCK_SIZE']), )
	add_kernel[grid](x, y, output, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE=64)
	return output

torch.manual_seed(8)
size = 8192
x = torch.rand(size, device="cuda:0")
y = torch.rand(size, device="cuda:0")
output_torch = x + y
outupt_triton = add(x, y)
torch.allclose(output_torch, output_triton, atol=1e-3, rtol=1e-3
```

Benchmarking it as below: 

```py
@triton.testing.perf_report(
	triton.testing.Benchmark(
		x_names = ['name'], 
		x_vals = [2**i for i in range(12, 28, 1)]
		x_log = True, 
		line_arg = 'provider', 
		line_vals = ['triton naive', 'torch']
		line_names = ['Triton Naive', 'Torch'], 
		styles  = ['Triton Naive', 'Torch'], 
		ylabel = 'GB/s', 
		plot_name = 'vector-add-performance', 
		args={}
		))
def benchmark(size, provider): 
	x = torch.rand(size, devie="cuda:0", dtype=torch.float32)
	y = torch.rand(size, device="cuda:0", dtype=torch.float32)
	quantiles = [0.5, 0.2, 0.8] 
	if provider == 'torch': 
		ms, min_ms, max_ms = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: x + y, quantiles= quantiles)
	if provider == 'triton naive': 
		ms, min_ms, max_ms = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: add(x, y), quantiles)
	
gbps = lambda ms: 3 * x.numel() * x.element_size() / ms * 1e-6

	return gbps(ms), gbps(max_ms), gbps(min_ms)


benchmark.run(print_data=True, show_plots=True)
```

Optimizing the vector add kernel with triton autotune

```py
@triton.autotune(
	configs=[
			triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE":128}, num_warps=2), 
			triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE": 256}, num_warps=4), 
			triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE": 512}, num_warps=4), 
			triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE": 1024}, num_warps=8), 
		], 
		key=['n_elements'], 
)

@triton.jit
def optimized_add_kernel(x_ptr
				y_ptr, 
				output_ptr, 
				n_elements, 
				BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr, 
				): 
	pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
	block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE 
	offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
	mask = offsets < n_elements
	x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask = mask) 
	y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask = mask) 
	output = x + y 
	tl.store(output_ptr + offsets, output, mask = mask)

```

Optimizations: 

- Larger block sizes   
- Multiple warps per block   
- Efficient grid mapping

Warp size and block size tends to heavily depend on GPU architecture. To deal with this variability triton came up with autotuning. Similar to how Cublass or cudnn internally select the best version for the GPU. 

Reduction kernels 

- Reduction is a common algorithmic operation used in parallel programming to reduce an array of N elements into a shorter array of elements or a single value. 

Definition of Naive Reduction Kernel

```py
@triton.jit
def reduce_kernel(
	x_ptr, 
	output_ptr, 
	n_elements, 
	BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr, 
): 
	pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
	block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
	
	acc = 0.0 
	for i in range(BLOCK_SIZE): 
		if (block_start + i) < n_elements: 	
			offset = block_start + i 
			mask = offset < n_elements 
			acc += tl.load(x_ptr + block_start + i, mask = mask)
	tl.atomic_add (output_ptr, acc)

```

![][image1]

Optimized Reduction Kernel with Tree Based Reduction within a Block. 

```py
@triton.autotune(
	configs=[
		triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE": 128}, num_warps=2), 
		triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE": 256}, num_warps=4), 
		triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE": 512}, num_warps=4), 
		triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE": 512}, num_warps=8),
		triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE": 1024}, num_warps=8), 
		triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE": 2048}, num_warps=8),
		triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE": 4096}, num_warps=8), 
		triton.Config({"BLOCK_SIZE": 8192}, num_warps=8),
		], 
		key = ["n_elements"], 
	)
@triton.jit
def reduce_kernel_optimized(x_ptr, out_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr): 
	pid = tl.program_id(0)
	offset = pid * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
	mask = offset < n_elements
	x = tl.load(x_ptr + offset, mask = mask, other = 0.0)

	block_sum = tl.sum(x, axis=0)
	tl.atomic_add(out_ptr, block_sum)
```

What are reasoning models?   
LLMs use next word predictions \- LLMs get distracted if the task or prompt is complex and this is where reasoning models help. It helpe take in a prompt split it into pieces and give the answer in reon \+ answer. Mimic humans thought process of doing it step by step instead of directly making it more trustworthy. This mimicking is called chain of Thought. It is basically when a model includes though process in its response, like human thinking.

- Reinforcement learning algorithm tailored for reasoning optizes policies like model reasoning and thinking looks at the content from the entire response scores groups of responses.   
- Training data \-\> Agent \-\> Ground truth which gives the rewards back to the agent.   
- GRPO treats the reasoning as a policy to be optimized.   
- Rewards are assignd

Evaluation Metrics 

- Time to first token (TTFT): The initial delay between sending and receiving the first piece of the output.   
- Time per output Token (TPOT): The average time it takes the AI to generate each new token after the first one.   
- Inter-Token Latency (ITL): The delay between the arrival of one token and the next on your screen.   
- End to End latency (E2EL): The total time from sending your request to receiving the entire completed response. 

LLM Preminaries

- Two broad approaches to improving an LLM   
  - Adjust the prompting  
  - Tune the Model (which changes the weights of the model)   
    - Tune and train are used as synonyms but train is done initially while tuning is done specifically for that particular model needs to be specialized for specific usecases.   
- Adjust the Prompting  
  - Treating LLM like a black box:   
- ![][image7]

Tune the Model 

- You show the model certain behaviour and the LLM learns from it. These weights can be thought of as neurons.   
- ![][image8]  
- 2 broad approaches to tuning   
  - Supervised fine tuning (SFT)  
  - Reinforcement Learning (RL)  
- ![][image9]  
- First we pass a batch of inputs to the LLM. Next we pass use the LLM to create a probability distribution for each next token. Each distribution can be thought of as a prediction, but we don’t sample from it to get our single next token.   
- Correct next token can alos be called a ground true token. Here we evaluate how likely it is and its corresponding distribution.   
- The model is updated to more probability on hte ground truth token. We can make it more heavily distributed towards the ground truth but that messes with the generalization. 

Compute hte Next Distributions  
Make the correct next token be fixed in Place

- Fix the ground truth token.   
- Compute the probability distribution and repeat.   
- Instead of calculating the distribution one step at a time we calculate the entire distribution at once.   
- We can actually do everything in parallel and we get all the ground truth tokens. We can make the LLM guess the distribution in parallel.   
- This is called teacher forcing?  
- IF we rely on previous distributions to come up with a new distribution it is called freerunning. Rarely done in practice and runs much slower. 

Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and sampling

- SFT worked on supplying inputs and targets. RL does not supply targets, insead RL just scores the predictions called rewards, higher the rewards more incentivised is the model to go with that answer. Rewards can be positive or negative.   
- Rewards can come from rules of thumbs incentivised to   
- In SFT you can compare any prediction to hte ground truth hence all comparisons are independent of each other.   
- RL has no ground truth and instead you should have the ability to score the whole output sequences. However you typically don’t have a good way to treat any single token. Which means you must sample sequences before they are scored. And we must do it one step at a time because later tokens depend on previous tokens.    
- RL training requires doing a step that looks just like inference where we sample outputs from the model before we update hte model.   
- In fact, it is common in RL to use inference engines like vLLM which are optimized to do the sampling.   
- ![][image10]

Module 3: RL Math  
How exactly is the model updated?

* Using the Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework.  
* We assume a timestep t, with state s(t) (the sequence generated so far), action a(t) (the next token), and θ as the parameters of our model. π(θ) is the probability distribution over actions given by our language model.  
* A(t) is the **advantage** — a measure of how much better an action was compared to what was expected (not the reward itself, though it's derived from rewards).  
  The gradient update is estimated using the **policy gradient**:  
* The exact expected value (over all possible sequences) is intractable to compute directly, so instead of calculating it exactly, we draw samples (rollouts) and use those to estimate it — this is the Monte Carlo approximation.  
* a(t) is a random variable, sampled from the distribution π(θ)(·|s(t)) — i.e., π(θ) tells us the probability of taking action a(t) given state s(t), according to the current model.  
* A(t) is a function of s(t) and a(t) — it reflects how good that specific action was in that specific state, relative to a baseline.  
* The core update direction is: **∇log π(θ)(a(t)|s(t)) × A(t)** — this is a single gradient vector (not "a distribution over gradients"). It points in the direction that increases the probability of actions with high advantage, and decreases the probability of actions with low/negative advantage.  
* In expectation (averaged across many sampled actions/states), this approximates the true gradient of the objective. In practice, we just average over a batch of sampled rollouts rather than computing the exact expectation.  
-   
- ![][image11]

**Formula 1 (top):**

E\_{a\_t \~ π\_θ(·|s\_t)} \[ A\_t · ∇\_θ log π\_θ(a\_t|s\_t) \]

* This says: take the expectation over actions a\_t, sampled from the policy π\_θ given state s\_t.  
* Inside the expectation: multiply the advantage A\_t by the gradient of the log-probability of that action.  
* In words: "on average, over all actions we could take from this state weighted by how likely the policy is to take them, push the parameters in the direction that increases probability of high-advantage actions."  
* This is the single-state, single-timestep version of the policy gradient.  
-   
- ![][image12]

**Formula 2 (nested expectation):**

E\_{State\_t \~ p\_θ(·)} \[ E\_{Act\_t \~ π\_θ(·|State\_t)} \[ adv\_θ(State\_t, Act\_t) · ∇\_θ log π\_θ(Act\_t|State\_t) \] \]

* This extends Formula 1 by also taking an expectation over states, not just actions.  
* p\_θ(·) is the distribution over states induced by the policy itself (since in autoregressive generation, which states you land in depends on which actions/tokens you sampled previously — the state distribution depends on θ).  
* The inner expectation is exactly Formula 1; the outer expectation averages that over all the states you might visit.  
* This combined form is often written compactly as a single joint expectation:

E\_{State\_t \~ p\_θ(·), Act\_t \~ π\_θ(·|State\_t)} \[ adv\_θ(State\_t, Act\_t) · ∇\_θ log π\_θ(Act\_t|State\_t) \]

**Formula 3 (Monte Carlo estimate — the practical version):**

(1/n) · Σ\_{s=1}^{len(seqs)} Σ\_{t=1}^{len(seqs\[s\])} adv\_θ(state\_{s,t}, act\_{s,t}) · ∇*θ log π\_θ(act*{s,t} | state\_{s,t})

* Since the expectation above is intractable to compute exactly (you can't enumerate every possible state/action pair), this is how it's actually computed in practice.  
* You sample n sequences (rollouts) — the outer sum over s from 1 to len(seqs) is looping over sequences.  
* Within each sequence, you loop over every timestep t (every token generated in that rollout) — the inner sum.  
* For each (state, action) pair you actually observed in your sampled rollouts, you compute the advantage and the gradient of the log-probability, and average all of these together.  
* This average is your **unbiased estimate** of the true expectation in Formula 2 — the Law of Large Numbers guarantees that as n (number of sampled sequences) grows, this average converges to the true expected value.  
* How is the state sampled?  
  * The state isn't independently sampled at random — it's built up **autoregressively**. At each timestep, the current state s(t) is the sequence of tokens generated so far (prompt \+ previously generated tokens).  
  * The model samples the next token a(t) from π(θ)(·|s(t)), that token gets appended to the sequence, and this becomes the new state s(t+1).  
  * This continues token-by-token until the sequence ends (e.g., an end-of-sequence token or max length), producing one full "rollout." Multiple rollouts are sampled this way to estimate the policy gradient.

Module 4: RL on Hardware 

- 2 trainings to do RL   
  - First we must sample rollouts  
  - Sampling can be done only one step at a time.   
  - Cuz we are sampling no gradients can be computed.   
- 2nd after sequences are produced and scored we run the token factor in a way that allows us to compute gradients. We can pass all tokens in parallel similar to SFT, because they all now exist.   
- There are many differences between the rollout phase and the update phase that effect how they run on hardware.   
- Rollout vs Update Phase.   
  - Rollout phase and update phase are using the same batch size. Using hte same batch size would either be too big for the update phase to fit in memory or too small for the rollout phase to roll out more efficiently.   
  - Memory bound, this means GPU spends most of its time stuck between the memory and the processor.   
  - Rollout phase can support larger batch sizes as it doesnt require using memory like backward graphs, gradients like the update phase does. One solution is to use bigger batch size for the rollout phase and a smaller batch size for the update phase.  
  - Unfortunately, this is a problem as this would mean the model would change for every batch. When we showed the model the next batch it shows a slightly modified version than what it would have produced this is called off policy data and leads to the model learning in an unstable way.   
- Optional Derivative of Importance Sampling  
  - ![][image13]  
  - This is the derivation of the **importance-sampling form of the policy gradient**, which is the foundation of PPO/GRPO-style RL updates. Here's the step-by-step logic:  
  - \*\*Row 1 — Vanilla policy gradient (REINFORCE)\*\*

  - Es∼pθ,a∼πθ\[advθ(s,a)∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s)\]E\_{s\\sim p\_\\theta, a\\sim\\pi\_\\theta}\[\\text{adv}\_\\theta(s,a)\\nabla\_\\theta \\log \\pi\_\\theta(a|s)\]Es∼pθ​,a∼πθ​​\[advθ​(s,a)∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s)\]  
  - This is the standard policy gradient: expectation over states/actions sampled from the \*current\* policy π\_θ, weighted by the advantage.  
  - **Row 2 — Expand the expectation over actions into an explicit sum**  
     The expectation over actions is rewritten as ∑aπθ(a∣s)⋅advθ(s,a)∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s)\\sum\_{a} \\pi\_\\theta(a|s) \\cdot \\text{adv}\_\\theta(s,a)\\nabla\_\\theta\\log\\pi\_\\theta(a|s) ∑a​πθ​(a∣s)⋅advθ​(s,a)∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s) — just making the sampling distribution explicit as a sum, no math change yet.  
  - **Row 3 — Multiply and divide by π\_θ\_old (importance sampling trick)**  
     Insert πθold(a∣s)πθold(a∣s)=1\\frac{\\pi\_{\\theta\_{old}}(a|s)}{\\pi\_{\\theta\_{old}}(a|s)} \= 1 πθold​​(a∣s)πθold​​(a∣s)​=1. This lets you reweight the expectation so it can later be taken under the *old* policy instead of the current one — the whole point being that you collected rollout data under π\_θ\_old, but want gradients w.r.t. the current π\_θ.  
  - **Row 4 — Regroup terms so π\_θ\_old is the sampling distribution**  
     Rearranged so πθold(a∣s)\\pi\_{\\theta\_{old}}(a|s) πθold​​(a∣s) sits outside as the distribution you're summing over, and πθ(a∣s)πθold(a∣s)\\frac{\\pi\_\\theta(a|s)}{\\pi\_{\\theta\_{old}}(a|s)} πθold​​(a∣s)πθ​(a∣s)​ becomes the importance weight (the ratio) multiplying everything else.  
  - **Row 5 — Convert the sum back into an expectation under the old policy**  
     Since πθold(a∣s)\\pi\_{\\theta\_{old}}(a|s) πθold​​(a∣s) is now the outer weighting term, the sum becomes an expectation over actions sampled from πθold\\pi\_{\\theta\_{old}} πθold​​ instead of πθ\\pi\_\\theta πθ​. This is the key move: **you can now use rollout data collected under the old policy to estimate gradients for the new policy**, via the importance ratio πθπθold\\frac{\\pi\_\\theta}{\\pi\_{\\theta\_{old}}} πθold​​πθ​​.  
  - **Row 6 — Rewrite ∇log using the identity ∇log f \= ∇f / f**  
     Substitute ∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s)=∇θπθ(a∣s)πθ(a∣s)\\nabla\_\\theta \\log \\pi\_\\theta(a|s) \= \\frac{\\nabla\_\\theta \\pi\_\\theta(a|s)}{\\pi\_\\theta(a|s)} ∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s)=πθ​(a∣s)∇θ​πθ​(a∣s)​. This introduces a 1πθ(a∣s)\\frac{1}{\\pi\_\\theta(a|s)} πθ​(a∣s)1​ term.  
  - \*\*Row 7 — Simplify: the π\_θ(a|s) terms cancel\*\*  
     The πθ(a∣s)\\pi\_\\theta(a|s) πθ​(a∣s) in the numerator (from the importance ratio) cancels with the 1πθ(a∣s)\\frac{1}{\\pi\_\\theta(a|s)} πθ​(a∣s)1​ from the log-derivative trick, leaving the clean final form (highlighted in red):

  - Es∼pθ, a∼πθold\[advθ(s,a)∇θπθ(a∣s)πθold(a∣s)\]E\_{s\\sim p\_\\theta,\\, a\\sim\\pi\_{\\theta\_{old}}}\\left\[\\text{adv}\_\\theta(s,a)\\frac{\\nabla\_\\theta \\pi\_\\theta(a|s)}{\\pi\_{\\theta\_{old}}(a|s)}\\right\]Es∼pθ​,a∼πθold​​​\[advθ​(s,a)πθold​​(a∣s)∇θ​πθ​(a∣s)​\]  
  - **Why this matters for your notes on rollout vs. update batch size:**  
     This derivation is *exactly* why RL training splits into rollout and update phases with potentially different batch sizes: the final expectation is sampled from πθold\\pi\_{\\theta\_{old}} πθold​​ (the rollout policy, frozen during generation), while gradients are computed w.r.t. the current πθ\\pi\_\\theta πθ​ during the update phase. The importance ratio ∇θπθπθold\\frac{\\nabla\_\\theta\\pi\_\\theta}{\\pi\_{\\theta\_{old}}} πθold​​∇θ​πθ​​ is what lets you decouple *when* you generate data from *when* you use it to update — which is also the mathematical justification for doing multiple gradient update steps (multiple mini-batches) per rollout batch, i.e., off-policy-ish PPO updates, as long as π\_θ hasn't drifted too far from π\_θ\_old (hence the clipping in PPO).

# **Module 6: PPO and GRPO**

## **Motivation: Why we need a baseline**

If the advantage estimate is always uniformly high (or always uniformly low) across all actions, the policy gradient struggles to discriminate — it can't tell *which* actions were good relative to others, since everything gets pushed in the same direction (just by different magnitudes). This makes learning slow and noisy.

**Solution:** subtract a baseline from the raw reward so the resulting advantage values cluster around 0\. This way, below-average actions get their probability pushed down (not just "less up"), and above-average actions get pushed up — a much sharper learning signal.

The model that estimates this baseline (an estimate of expected return from a state) is called the **critic** or **value function model**.

---

## **PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization)**

**The problem PPO solves:** unconstrained importance-sampling updates can move π\_θ arbitrarily far from π\_θ\_old in a single step, causing instability (the ratio r(θ) \= π\_θ/π\_θ\_old can blow up or collapse).

### **Z-shaped clipping — the intuition**

* Clip the ratio r(θ) only when it moves too far (beyond \[1−ε, 1+ε\]) **in the direction of increasing the objective**.  
* If r(θ) is small (policy moving away from a good action) — don't clip, since we still want the gradient to correct this.  
* If r(θ) is large but the update is *moving back toward* π\_θ\_old (i.e., self-correcting) — don't clip either, since this isn't a problematic drift.  
* **We only clip updates that push us further away from π\_θ\_old by more than ε.** Updates that move us *back toward* π\_θ\_old are always allowed through unclipped.

This asymmetric behavior is achieved by taking the **min** of the unclipped and clipped objective:

**L\_PPO \= E\[ min( adv\_θ · r(θ), adv\_θ · clip(r(θ), 1−ε, 1+ε) ) \]**

* **Positive advantage:** the min creates a flat ceiling once r(θ) exceeds 1+ε — extra upside from over-updating is discarded, but there's no floor, so downward corrections are never blocked.  
* **Negative advantage:** the min creates a flat floor once r(θ) drops below 1−ε — but no ceiling, so the policy is always free to correct back upward.

This gives PPO its "proximal" property: it discourages large policy updates without fully preventing self-correcting ones.

---

## **GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization)**

**Origin:** introduced by DeepSeek.

**Problem with the standard critic approach:** computing the advantage via a learned baseline normally requires training a *separate* value/critic model concurrently with the policy — doubling compute and adding complexity.

**GRPO's fix:** eliminate the critic entirely.

* For each input prompt, sample **multiple rollouts**	 (multiple completions) from the current policy.  
* This set of completions for one input is called a **group**.  
* Instead of a learned baseline, **normalize the rewards within the group**: subtract the group mean and divide by the group standard deviation, so each response's advantage reflects how it did *relative to its siblings* (mean 0, std 1).

### **Full GRPO objective**

(1/G) Σᵢ₌₁..G (1/|oᵢ|) Σₜ₌₁..|oᵢ| { min\[ (π\_θ(o\_i,t|q,o\_i,\<t) / π\_θ\_old(o\_i,t|q,o\_i,\<t)) · Â\_i,t , clip(π\_θ(o\_i,t|q,o\_i,\<t) / π\_θ\_old(o\_i,t|q,o\_i,\<t), 1−ε, 1+ε) · Â\_i,t \] − β·D\_KL\[π\_θ‖π\_ref\] }

Key structural points:

* **G** \= number of rollouts (group size) per prompt; sums/averages the PPO-style clipped objective over all responses in the group and over all tokens in each response.  
* **Â\_i,t** \= the group-normalized advantage (same for all tokens in a given response i, since GRPO typically assigns a single scalar reward per full response).  
* A **KL penalty term** (β·D\_KL\[π\_θ‖π\_ref\]) is added directly into the loss, penalizing divergence from a fixed reference policy — this replaces the separate reward-shaping KL penalty used in some PPO/RLHF setups and adds a second layer of stability on top of the clipping.

**Net effect:** GRPO gets a variance-reduced advantage estimate (like a critic would provide) purely from sampling statistics within a group — no separate value network to train, which is the main efficiency win over vanilla PPO for LLM RLHF.

MOdule 7: Modern Reinforcement Learning GSPO (QWEN team) and SAPO

- GSPO: Weight & Clip Based on Whole Sequences  
  - GRPO is unstable and clipping was probably the issue.   
  - ![][image19]  
  - KL divergence seems gone but its still there. Probability divergence appears to be clipped instead of probability ratios of individual tokens  
  - Each sequence probability ratio is normalized by its length.   
  - It showed more clipping   
  - Does this clipping result in lower efficiency?   
    - NO\!  
    - This counter intuitive findingthat clipping a much larger fraction of tokens leads to superior training further indicates that GRPOs token level gradient estimates are inherently noisy.   
    - These merits of GSPO ultimately contributed to the exceptional performance improvements in the latest QWEN3 models.   
- ![][image20]  
- Routing replay was required before this but with this routing replay was not required.   
- Is hard clipping too abrupt?   
  - Positive Advantage with clip parameter epsilon \= 1\.   
  -   
- ![][image21]  
- They used SAPO instead.   
-   
- 

SAPO (Soft adaptive policy optimization): Soft gate

- ![][image22]  
- ![][image23]  
- Instead of falling abruptly you have a asmooth drop off depeding on the temperature. Lower the temperature smoother is the drop off. Notice in the chart how the temperature can cause the objective value to shift upwards. Higher temperature means faster drop off which means negative advantage tokens causes a lot of instability.   
- Is this going back to sequence level view instead of token level?   
  - No\!  
  - Under mild assumptions it turns out the soft gate of SAPO behaves similar to the sequence level hard clip like GSPO.   
  - Assumption 1: small on policy steps  
  - Assumption 2: Low dispersion of token log-ratios within a sequence.   
  - ![][image24]

So the loop is really: current weights → produce a probability distribution → sample rollouts from it → score them → use the relative rewards to compute a gradient → update the weights → distribution shifts slightly (higher-reward tokens/paths now more probable) → repeat.

Attention Sinks 

- Are specific tokens often hte first few that attract disproportionate attention in transformer models due to softmax normalization of attentin weights. This acts as an anchor in attention distribution.

- When early tokens are evicted from the KV cache the model loses anchor for stable attention, thequality degrades rapidly. While keeping this sinc tokens efficiently while evicting most others models can produce good output even with sliding window attention or long streaming context.  
- Prefix caching allows computing KV cache across requests with common prefixes like system prompts. However this requires evicting old cache  entries when memory fills up. But prefix caching with eviction needs to protect attention sinks. Tokens AITER currently doesn’t support or identify tokens during cache eviction  
- Async\_scheduling \- Works asynchronously. In times of high load this is essential.

- HIP\_FORCE\_DEV\_KERNARG \- by default kernel arguments are copied from host memory to GPU by default this is a small win per kernel  
- Sliding window is done to avoid KV cache from exploding.

  - NCCL\_SOCKET\_IFNAME=eth0 \- high performance counterpart for GLOO, GLOO handles the administrative side of the processes. NCCL is the NVIDIA collective communications library that handles the heavy lifting of moving the actual data. In AMD they use RCCL it is similar to NCCL.

Module 5: Optimization Options for Deepseek-R1 70B and Benchmarking the implementation

- Optimizing the KV cache fp 16 kv cache can be reduced to 8 bit fp to allow more concurrent users and longer sequences. However there is a hidden cost even this increases tokens per second, if you only have one or few users then you are basically adding latency to convert hte fp16 to fp8 on the fly thus its important to really understand your user base and how they are using your infrastructure.   
- Next flag is the gpu-memory-utilization normally by default it is 0.9 but you can increase it manually to other higher values for better performance.   
- The rest of the 0.1 of the GPU would be used for HIP Graphs, HIP Graphs is a workflow of multiple GPU operations fused into one action. An LLM will have one for every input size and precache to speed things up. Costs about 6 to 8 GB. If you don’t leave room for them recording can take a long time. Second, fragmented memory, Unaligned variable space used by Pytorch adding another 2 to 4 GB. Thrid, is the kernel workspace, temporary storage space for Matmul operations. Costs 1 to 2 GB.   
- Chunked prefill: be default its enabled to make multiple concurrent users prioritizing raw throughput over latency considerations.

OF course the last optimization is AITER (AI tensor engine for ROCM) and the switch turns it on. If it is turned off it will use vllm generic pytorch code. When its on it uses triton code or code which is specific for that architecture speeding up lower level operations. So its good to turn it off.   
![][image37]  
That flag does a few key things under the hood:   
![][image38]  
The flag enables a fused GPU kernel which combines  2 key optimizations during inference.   
To quantizing FPA KV cache values. The model stores Keys and values in 8 bit precision to save memory before using them for attention we need to conver them back to higher precision. Applying Rope, rotary position embedding, which tells the model the order of tokens. Transformers process all tokens in parallel. RoPE rotates each vector based on its position encoding relative distance between the attention and its relative calculation. Normally these 2 operations run separately. Kernel handles the math automatically.   
Export VLLM\_ROCM\_USE\_AITER\_LINEAR=1 \- basically improves linear calculations especially in the Q, K, V layers. Normally these matrics multiplications use math routines. While correct they are not fully optimized for AMD GPUs. The flag maximizes throughput and minimize latency. A lot of time   
Export TORCH\_BLAS\_PREFER\_HIPBLASLT=1

- LLM spend a lot of time on Matrix multiplications. Especially the GEMM matrix and attention operations and feedforward layers, these operations form the backbone of transformer inference and where the heavy computation happens.   
- On AMD RoCM there are multiple libraries that provide these operations such as rocBLAS and hipBLASlt  optimized for rocm GPUs

`TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_HIPBLASLT=1` tells PyTorch to use AMD's newer hipBLASLt library instead of rocBLAS for matrix multiplications, which is typically faster for the low-precision (bf16/fp8) matmuls that dominate LLM inference.
