HIP Porting Foundations

- Objectives   
  - Apply Heterogeneous computing interface for Portability (HIP) programming concepts to port, build and validate GPU applications across platforms.   
- HIP Porting: What and Why   
  - HIP functions as a C++ marshalling interface that maps to either the ROCm (AMD GPUs) or CUDA (NVIDIA GPUs) platform.   
  - Why porting is required:   
    - AMD and NVIDIA GPUs use different ISAs and code formats. (.hsaco / .hip\_fatbing vs .ptx / .cubin / .fatbin)  
    - Device binary are nto interchangeable.   
    - Same source \-\> must be compiled per platform.   
  - What HIP enables:   
    - CUDA like programming sematnics.   
    - Unified Runtime APIs  
    - CUDA splits responsibilities between cu\* driver vs .cuda\* runtime.   
    - Mirroring of CUDA driver/runtime (modules, contexts, streams, events)  
  - How porting works  
    - Incremental migration of CUDA \-\> HIP conversion.   
    - Compilation with NVIDIA nvcc via AMD hipcc.   
    - Platform specific binaries generated.   
- A pragmatic workflow  
  - Step 1: Scan with HIPIFY –examine to quantify API references, LOC and warnings.   
  - Step 2: Convert using hipify-clang (AST-based) where buildable; use hipify-perl for quick/partial conversions. (hipify-perl for quick conversions while hipify-clang for in depth conversions).   
  - Step 3: Validate on NVIDIA hardware first via hipcc \-\>nvcc to stabilize functionality and performance.   
  - Step 4: Guard platform specifics with \_\_HIP\_PLATFORM\_AMD\_\_ / \_\_HIP\_PLATFORM\_NVIDIA\_\_ . These make the compiler skip the code.   
  - Step 5: Build for AMD with HIP-Clang/amdclang++; validate on ROCm GPUs and tune occupancy.   
  - Step 6: Iterate scan \-\> convert \-\>build; resolve nested includes, wrappers, context/module corner cases.   
- HIPIFY Tooling (clang vs perl)  
  - Hipify clang (recommended for Production)  
    - Clang based AST parsing   
    - Accurate for complex code   
    - CUDA headers required   
  - Hipify perl (Quick scane & SImple code)   
    - Pattern based text substitution.   
    - No CUDA install required   
    - Simpler setup.   
- Supporting Modes:   
  - –examine \-\>estimate conversion coverage. Basically shows which files cna be changed and any warnings about hte code and the command you used as well as the apis which can be changed.   
  - Directory scripts \-\> [hipexamine.sh](http://hipexamine.sh) & [hipexamine-perl.sh](http://hipexamine-perl.sh). These supports large scale source tree analysis.  
  - Conversion \-\> –inplace & [hipconvertinplace.sh](http://hipconvertinplace.sh) create auto-backup. –inplace & [hipconversioniinplace.sh](http://hipconversioniinplace.sh)  modify source files directly while preserving .prehipbackups.   
  - Reports: detailed stats like APIs, counts, LOC, warnings helping identify amnual intervention points.   
- Build and Toolchain Essentials   
  - 

|  | AMD | NVIDIA |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| hipcc | Amdclang++ (HIP-clang-path) | Nvcc  |
| Binaries  | Not portable \- compile for AMD target  | Not portable \- compile for NVIDIA target.  |
| hipconfig | Used to query platform, compiler, include paths, and runtime.  | Used to query platform compiler, include paths, and runtime. q |
| Headers  | hip/hip\_runtime.h (superset) preferred over hip/hip\_runtime\_api.h(subset | Nvcc often auto-includes CUDA headers.  |
| Platform | \_\_HIP\_Platform\_AMD\_ | \_\_HIP\_PLATFORM\_NVIDIA |
| PTX Just in time Compilation | Not implemented \- hipModuleLoadDataEx behaves like hipModuleLoadData |  |
|  |  |  |

- Platform and Pass detection (Macro reference table)

Compilation Passes: 

| Macro | amdclang++ | Nvcc (hipcc backend) | Other (GCC/MSVC/Clang) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| \_\_HIP\_PLATFORM\_AMD\_\_ | Defined | Undefined | Must define explicitly |
| \_\_HIP\_PLATFORM\_NVIDIA | Undefined | Defined | Must define explicitly |
| \_\_HIPCC\_\_/\_\_HIP\_\_ | Defined for HIP inputs | Defined for HIP inputs | Must define explicitly |
| \_\_HIP\_\_DEVICE\_COMPILE\_\_ | 1 on device pass  | 1 on device pass.  | Undefined.  |
| \_\_CUDACC\_\_, \_\_NVCC\_\_ | Undefined | Defined | Undefined |
| \_\_CUDA\_ARCH\_\_ | Undefined | Defined (device only) | Undefined |
| Note: HIP feature-specific macros recommended over \_\_CUDA\_ARCH\_\_ |  |  |  |

- Amdclang++ performs multiple device passes (per GPU target)  
- Nvcc performs a host pass \+ a single device pass \- use \_\_HIP\_DEVICE\_COMPILE\_\_. 

Modules and Code Objects 

- 

| Artifact  | APIs  | Nvcc  | HIP-CLang |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Code Object  | hipModuleLoad, hipModuleLoadData | .cubin or PTX  | .hsaco |
| Fat Binary | hipMOduleLoadFatBin | .fatbin | .hip\_fatbin |

- No cross-vendor fatbin-build seperately for AMD and NVIDIA.   
- Both backends support embedding code objects in the executable and dynamic loading via hipModuleLoad\*   
- NVCC PTX JIT option: hipModuleLoadDataEx passes PTX-JIT options on NVIDIA, ignored on AMD (.hsaco is fully compiled).   
- **Fat binary:** a single file bundling compiled GPU code for several architectures, so the runtime can pick the one that matches the GPU it finds.  
- **Code object:** the compiled GPU code for one specific architecture (e.g. `gfx942`), which is what `hipModuleLoadData` loads.

HIP-Clang Runtime: What happens at Load

- Device linking: HIP-Clang links device code across translation units \- bundles per target code into \_\_hip\_fatbin ELF section   
- Init/term Functions   
  - Auto generated host init calls   
    - \_\_hipRegisterFatBinary   
    - \_\_hipRegisterFunction   
    - \_\_hipRegisterVar  
  - Termination call   
    - \_\_hipUnregisterFatBinary  
- Single Regitster Guard  
  - Global \_\_hip\_\_gpubin\_handle (linkonce, void\*\*=0) ensures one-time registration. 

Result: Stubs are associated with kernels ready for \<\<\<\>\>\> or hipModuleLaunchKernel

Kernel launch Mechanics (HIP-Clang)

- HIP Supports three kernel launch forms   
- Triple chevron syntax \<\<\<\>\>\>   
- hipLaunchKernel   
- hipLaunchKernelGGL ( a macro can expand to \<\<\<\>\>\> by default-can become template to HIP\_TEMPLATE\_KERNEL\_LAUNCH)  
- HIP Host side Kernel Launch Sequence.   
- hipConfigureCall: Sets the grid, block, dynamic shared memory and stream.   
- hipSetupArgument\*: Packs kernel arguments.   
- hipLaunchByPtr: Dispatches kernel  
- Context is basically grouping of one process in a GPU or my processes working state in a GPU

|  | CUDA | HIP/HIP-Clang |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Contexts | \-Explicit and multiple contexts hosted per device  \- Each device has its own streams, events, virtual address space, and memory pointers \- you *can* create several contexts on one GPU, for example two independent "sessions" in one process, each with its own memory and streams. | Manual creation avoided  hipSetDevice() and streams used for execution control you don't. There's effectively one context per GPU, and you use streams to keep work separate.		 |
| Address Spaces | Per-context device address spaces used a pointer from `cudaMalloc` in context A means nothing in context B. | Process-wide address space used \- pointers are shareable across contexts.  Primary contexts created on first use- mixing runtime and driver calls can differe from CUDA.  the pointer is valid anywhere in the process. |
| Deprecations |  | hipCtx\* exists for porting but deprecated for new development.  |

- Action: Favor runtime API and streams; avoid new hipCtx\*; review mixed API code during migration. 

Memory Copies, Pointer Attributes and Directionality 

- Memory Copies:   
  - Direction specific APIs:   
    - hipMemcpyHtoD   
    - hipMemcpyDtoH  
    - hipMemcpyDtoD  
  - Generic hipMemcpy(ptr, kind)  
  - Overhead reduced by using explicit direction calls(transfer path known at compile time).   
- Pointer Attributes:   
  - Queried with hipPointerGetAttributes(), whose attr.type reports whether pointer to host, device, array or managed memory.   
  - HIP and CUDA enumerations 

| HIP | CUDA |
| :---- | :---- |
| hipMemoryType | cudaMemoryType |
|  | cudaMemoryTypeUregistered.  |

  - NVIDIA platform: HIP headers/runtime map these enums on nvidia\_hip\_runtime\_api.h  
  - HIP enums aren't identical on AMD and NVIDIA, so a `switch` on them can fail to compile on one platform. Wrap the platform-specific cases in `#ifdef __HIP_PLATFORM_AMD__` / `__HIP_PLATFORM_NVIDIA__`.  
- Directionality   
  - Identify the correct pointer type to avoid misclassifying memory and prevent incorrect copy directions or unexpected transfer behaviour.   
  - Ensures the runtime sees the correct memory type to avoid direction errors and simplify debugging. 

Module 2: HIP Porting Best Practices: Advanced Portability, Debugging Aids, and Migration

Objective: Apply advanced HIP portability techniques, including warp size handling, feature macros, library selection, launch bounds,, and memory introspection and use debugging aids and the migration checklist to ensure correct cross-platform execution. 

Warp Size Portability 

- Do not assume warpsize is 32 lanes (NVIDIA) or 32/64 lanes (AMD architectures, including RDNA GPUs)  
- Device Code: Reference the warpSize builtin variable   
- Host: Query device properties at runtime to obtain warpSize   
- Update lane-mask logic to use a width that covers both cases (for example, uint64\_t)  
- Define lan\_mask\_t that adapts to the active warp width. 

```c
# if defined(__GFX8__) || defined(__GFX9__) 
typedef uint64_t lane_mask_t; 
#else 
typedef uint32_t lane_mask_t; 
#endif

//Get the thread's position in the warp. 
unsigned int laneId = threadIdx.x % warpSize; 

// Use lane ID for bit-shift
val & ((lane_mask_t{1} << (threadIdx.x % warpSize)) -1); 

//Shift 32 or 64 bit integer with val variable; 
WarpReduce::sum((val < warpsize)? (lane_mask{1} << val) : 0);
```

Portable Feature Gating (Device and Host) 

| Device Side Macros  | Host Side macros  |
| :---- | :---- |
| Use \_\_HIP\_ARCH\_HAS\_\<FEATURE\>\_\_ macros to include or exclude code that requires specific hardware features.  | Do not rely on device macros because actual GPUs may differ at runtime.  Use hipGetDeviceProperties or hipDeviceGetAttribute |
| Examples  \_\_HIP\_ARCH\_HAS\_DOUBLES\_\_ \_\_HIP\_ARCH\_HAS\_GLOBAL\_INT64\_ATOMICS\_\_ \_\_HIP\_ARCH\_HAS\_WARP\_SHUFFLE\_\_ \_\_HIP\_ARCH\_HAS\_3DGRID\_\_ \_\_HIP\_ARCH\_HAS\_DYNAMIC\_PARALLEL\_\_ | Examples  hasDoubles  hasWarpShuffle has3DGrid hasSharedInt32Atomics |

Avoid using \_\_CUDA\_ARCH\_\_, which is CUDA specific and non-portable outside of NVIDIA.   
Feature Macros to Host Capability probability.   
Libraries: hip\* (Portable) vs .roc\* (AMD-Optimized) 

| hip\* LIbraries  | roc\* libraries |
| :---- | :---- |
| Portable marshalling layers that route to roc\* on AMD or CUDA libraries on NVIDIA | AMD Optimized, may include ISA specific kernels or alternate APIs, not intended as portable abstractions.  |

Strategy   
Step 1: For cross vendor deployment, standardize on hip\* interfaces  
Step 2: For AMD GPU-only solutions, use roc\* where available.  
Step 3: When targeting AMD exclusively, use HIPIFY –roc to bias mapping toward roc\*.   
Runtime vs Driver Launches 

- Preferable runtime \<\<\<\>\>\> kernel launches for simplicity and readability .  
- 

| Driver style APIs (hipModule\*) | NVIDIA |
| :---- | :---- |
| hipModuleLoad \- dynamic code loading	 hipModuleGetFunction \- retrieving kernel symbols from modules hipModuleLaunchKernel \- launching requires explicit parameters buffers.  | On NVIDIA backends, flows may mirror CUDA driver initialization and start with hipInit and hipCtxCreate before module operations.  |

- Note: Ensure the code object (.ptx / .cubin vs hsaco) matches the backend and kernel names passed to hipModuleGetFunction are correct. 

Porting\_launch\_bounds\_\_  
CUDA\_\_launch\_bounds\_\_ (MAX\_THREADS\_PER\_BLOCK, MIN\_BLOCKS\_PER\_MULTIPROCESSOR) sets a block size constraint and a minimum blocks per streaming processor

| CU Mode (CDNA) Formula | WGP Mode (RDNA) Fomula |
| :---- | :---- |
| MIN\_WARPS\_PER\_EXECUTION\_UNIT \= (MIN\_BLOCKS\_PER\_MULTIPROCESSOR \* MAX\_THREADS\_PER\_BLOCK) / (warpSize \*2) | MIN\_WARPS\_PER\_EXECUTION\_UNIT \= (MIN\_BLOCKS\_PER\_MULTIPROCESSOR \* MAX\_THREADS\_PER\_BLOCK) / (warpSIze \* 4\) |

HIP uses launch-bounds based occupancy control rather than –maxregcount compiler flag. 

| Driver Entry Points | Per-thread Default Stream  |
| :---- | :---- |
| hipGetProcAddress to obtain runtime function pointers dynamically 	 Use cases include feature probing, forward compatibility and plugin architecture.  Driver vs Runtime Resolution hipGetProcaddress and cuGetProcAddress aligns with the driver.  hipGetDriverEntryPoint and cudaGetDriverEntryPoint exposes runtime API entry points	 | hipStreamPerThread to reduce contention and simplify asynchronous command submission.  Paired with operations like hipMemsetAsync and explicitly hipStreamSynchronize on the same per-thread stream to enforce ordering.  |

Memory Type Introspection (HIP vs CUDA)

- Integrate pointer classification checks into memory management utilities by using hipPointerGetAttributes (\&attr, ptr) and branching on attr.type.   
- 

| Memory Type Enumerations | HIP Examples | CUDA Examples  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Host  | hipMemoryTypeHost | cudaMemoryTypeHost |
| Device  | hipMemoryTypeDevice | cudaMemoryTypeDevice |
| Managed | hipMemoryTypeManaged | cudaMemoryTypeManaged |
| Unregistered |  | cudaMemroyUnregistered |

- Application code that switches over enum values should use \#ifdef \_\_HIP\_PLATFORM\_AMD\_\_ or \#ifdef \_\_HIP\_PLATFORM\_NVIDIA\_\_ to avoid mismatches. 

Common Pitfalls and Debugging Aids

- Header Gaps  
  - Check for includes after HIPIFY –nvcc auto-includes CUDA headers; HIP requires explicit includes.   
- CUDA\_ARCH Usage: Replace with HIP feature macros and host queries.   
- Warp Assumptions: Do not hard code 32 lanes; use warpSize and 64-bit masks.   
- Context Mixing: Account for HIP Clang primary context push; test runtime/driver paths.   
- Module Mismatches: Match .hsaco vs .ptx verify symbols with hipModuleGetFunction  
- Memory Transfer: Use hipPointerAttributes and assertions in debug builds. 

Migration Checklist: 

- Run with HIPIFY (--examine) and capture references, total lines and warnings.   
- Convert using hipify-clang or hipify-perl as appropriate, then rescan and rebuild   
- Validate on NVIDIA(hipcc \-\> nvcc); fix logic and performance issues and introduce platform guards.   
- Compile on AMD with HIP-Clang; validate kernels, memory paths and occupancy.   
- Feature gate device code with HIP\_ARCH\_HAS\* and query device properties on host.   
- Decide a library strategy (use hip\* for portability or roc\* for AMD GPU-specific optimization)  
- Hand off module format documentioation build configurations and a CI matrix per platform (.ptx / .cubin / .fatbin for NVIDIA and .hsaco / .hip\_fatbin for AMD). 

Summary 

- Successful migration depends on understanding platform specific behaviours such as macros, launch semantics and memory handling \- to ensure correct and efficient execution on both GPU architectures. 

	  
amdclang++ performs multiple device passes (one per GPU target); nvcc performs a host pass plus a single device pass  
Objectives 

- Explain how ROCgdb enables unified CPU-GPU debugging on RDNA architectures.   
- Apply wavefront and lane level debugging suing breakpoints stepping and memory inspection  
- 

Rocgdb Architecture Overview 

- Purpose: Unified GDB based debugger for CPU and AMDGPU code on the ROCm platform.   
- ![][image40]  
- Gdb is for frontend, AMD GPU specifics for backend. The MADGPU Target Backend execution semantics (waves, lanes, dispatch states).   
- Rocgdpapi \- Interacts with the GPU at a low level to inspect runtime program state.   
- The api interacts with these agents to provide visibility into kernel execution, registers, memory and thread behaviour.   
- Backend translates the standard debugging commands into GPU aware operations, bridging host debugging with GPU hardware control. 

RDNA GPU Targets and HIP Debug Build 

- Target Ids: Use gfx architecture specific (gfx1100, gfx1151, gfx1200)  
- Compilation flags: Compile HIP code with \-g, \-O0 and –offload-arch=\<gfx\>. \-g and \-O0 are debug flags   
- Generic Targets use gfx11 or gfx12 if the exact GPU SKU is unknown   
- Verify Hardware: Confirm the GPU architecture using the rocminfo tool.   
- Debugging settings: enable debug symbols and disable aggressive optimizations for accurate source level debugging.  
- Toolchain compatibility: Ensure HIP Toolchain and ROCm versions match the GPUs supported targets.   
- Environment validation: Verify toolchain with hipcc –version and rocgdb –version.

ROCgdb: Debugging CPU \+ GPU Together (Steps)

- HIP APplication (CPU \+ GPU Kernel) \- CPU acts as the host agent \- GPUs act as execution agents.   
- COmpile with Debug (Using \-g, \-O0)  
- Launch ROCgdb \-\> CPU Debug/GPU Debug Standard GDB commands used. Kernel level debugging enabled at the wavefront and lane levels.   
- ROCgdb Backend \-\> RODdbgapi both communicate directly with AMD hardware   
- RDNA GPU HW. 

AMDGPU Execution Topology (Conceptual Map). 

- Queue \-\> Dispatch \-\> Work-groups \-\> Wavefront \-\> Lanes  
- Queue \- Command submission from the host to the GPU.   
- Dispatch Kernel launch (parallel execution instance).   
- Work-groups \- Scheduled across compute units to execute portions of the workload in parallel.   
- Wavefront \- Groups of threads executed in lockstep (debugger-visible unit).   
- Lanes \- INdividual work-item executing in lockstep.   
- Wavefront and lane behavior in RDNA   
  - Execution model: RDNA architecture uses wavefronts: Multiple lanes execute in lok-step (SIMT model)  
  - Single program counter is shared by all lanes in a wavefront.   
  - Control Flow and divergence   
  - Divergence: Active/inactive lane masks used.   
  - Lane masks control active execution and exposes divergence behaviour during execution.   
  - Register Model: SGPRs are shared by the entire wavefront.   
    - VGPRs are lane specific  
  - Debugging with ROCgdb   
    - Selecting and inspecting lanes via lanes indices.   
    - Observing lane masks and behaviour to identify indexing issues and debug kernels.   
- Device code loading and symbol resolution:   
  - Compilation and launch: HIP Kernels are compiled into AMDGPU device code objects   
  - Setting breakpoints: Device code not loaded \- breakpoints remain pending.   
  - Kernel Dispatch: Breakpoints set before load remain pending.   
    - ROCgdb loads the code object and resolves pending breakpoints.   
  - Execution Begins Wave hits breakpoint- STOP:   
    - First wave reaching a breakpoint stops execution.   
    - Multiple waves may hit the same breakpoint afterward.   
    - Use conditions or disable breakpoints to reduce noise. 

Breakpoints for Host and Device 

- Breakpoints follow a unified model across host and device while maintaining standard GDB semantics.   
- Host Breakpoints  
  - Behave as in traditional CPU debugging   
- Device Breakpoints   
  - Can be set on kernel functions or specific lines in GPU code. 

Device code loads at kernel dispatch- ROCgdb may mark unresolved breakpoints as pending until the device code loads. 

- Multiple wavefronts from the same dispatch may hit the same breakpoint, causing repeated stops.  
- Active Breakpoints \- Inspect using info breakpoints and manage with enable, disable or delete operations.    
- Conditional Breakpoints \- Target specific threads or lanes to improve debugging focus.   
- Disable Breakpoints \- Reduce noise and ensure a more controlled debugging workflow. 

Selecting and Inspecting Waves. 

- Use the info threads command to view both CPU and GPU wavefronts. \- Listing execution contexts   
- Find the GPU wave labeled with its queue, dispatch and execution context \- identifying the Target Wave   
- Use thread \<id\> to select the corresponding GPU wave (thread).   
- Select specific wave to prevent context switches among multiple waves, ensuring consistent behaviour \- Stabilizing Execution 	  
- Follow the single execution path \- this focused context is required before inspecting lane-level behaviour. \- Inspecting the Wave. 

Selecting and Inspecting Lanes 

- Lane-level inspection: Fine-grained visibility into GPU execution within a wavefront.   
- Use info lanes to display per-lane activity, including execution state and register values. \- per lane activity.   
- Use lane \<n\> to select specific work-item \- select a Lane   
- Inspect VGPR values (lane specific) to examining local data and per thread computation \- VGPR inspection  
- Use to indicate active lanesduring divergence; observe mask changes to reveal divergence patterns & debug issues \- Lane masks  
- Combine lane selection wih conditional breakpoints for targeting debugging. \- combine tools. 

Source level debugging on GPU

- Step \-\> Next \-\> Finish \-\>Continue   
- Step: Advances active lanes within a wave \- divergent lanes remain inactive until reconvergence.   
- Next: Steps over function calls within the same wavefront   
- Skips entering runtime / helper functions   
- Finish: Exits runtime/helper functions cleanly and returns to the caller context.   
- Continue: Resumes execution until the next breakpoint \- multiple wavefronts may hit the breakpoints.   
- To ensure accurate source level debugging   
  - Compile with \-O0 to preserve source level mapping.   
  - Understand that GPU execution is asynchronous \- behaviour reflects synchronization points, not strict sequential execution.   
  - Adopt a wave centric execution model rather than a thread centric approach. 

Source \-\> ISA Mapping

- Allows developers to correlate HIP source code with AMDGPU instructions.   
- Disassemble /m: Mixed source and ISA representation.   
- DWARF Validation: Source-line associations correctly reflect the executed instructions  
- DWARF validation checks that the debug info's mapping between GPU instructions and source lines is accurate, so the line the debugger shows matches the instruction actually executing.  
- ISA Level: Deeper insight into divergence or complex control flow.   
  - Hidden execution paths and optimizations exposed.   
- Note: Avoid text user interface (TUI) mode \- use standard terminal views for mixed disassembly.

Registers and Execution States. 

- Register access   
  - Use info registers to inspect SGPR and VGPR values   
  - SGPRs values are shared across the wavefront and hold uniform data  
  - VGPRs values vary per land and require lane selection   
  - Program counter (PC): Shared across all lanes in a wavefront (lock-step execution)  
  - EXEC Mask: Indication of active / inactive lanes, crucial for control flow divergence.   
  - Analyze register values and masks to validate index computations.   
  - Modify register values but uses this capability cautiously as it can affect execution correctness. 

Memory Inspection Across Address Spaces. 

- Inspect Memory: Uses print and x/ \<format\> to inspect address spaces (e.g., x/16gf \<ptr\> to examine floating point data).  
  - Global memory: Most commonly inspected \- holds kernel input/output.   
  - LDS.scratch memory: Correct addressing and context selection essential, as tey are scoped per work group or lane.   
- Validate Indexing: Validate data indexing before assuming memory corruption.   
- Compare results: Compare memory values before and after kernel execution to verify correctness.   
- Synchronize properly: Ensure host and device synchronization before inspecting memory to avoid stale or incomplete data.   
- Inspect Memory \-\> Validate Indexing \-\> Compare Values \-\> Synchronize Properly

Exceptions, Faults and precision debugging

- ROCgdb detects GPU-side exceptions (memory faults, ALU errors) during kernel execution   
- Faults:   
  - Precise reporting with set amdgpu precise-memory on command   
  - Useful for identifying invalid memory accesses or incorrect computations.   
  - Fault may not appear immediately at the point of occurrence due to asynchronous GPU execution   
- How to Diagnose these faults: Inspect lane-level state to identify faulty executionpath   
  - Use smaller workloads toimprove reproducibility.   
  - Combine ISA level inspection with breakpoints for detailed analysis. 

Best RDNA Debugging

- Compile \-g, \-O0, –offload-arch-\<gfx\>  
- Use conditional breakpoints to reduce multi-wave noise   
- Focus debugging on a single wave then on a specific lane.   
- Narrow scope systematically: wave \-\> lane \-\> index.   
- Disable breakpoints after first meaningful hit.   
- Combine source, ISA and lane views for full visibility   
- Use deterministic inputs and smaller workloads.   
- Keep ROCm platform, HIP and ROCgdb versions aligned. 

Summary 

- ROCgdb enables heterogeneous debugging by exposing GPU execution at the wave and lane levels alongside CPU threads   
- Correct build settings (-g, \-O0, –offload-arch=\<gfx\>) and an understanding of the RDNA execution hierarchy are essential for effective debugging.   
- Debugging GPU issues analyzing divergence, indexing and memory behaviour at the lane level. 

VGPR values varya per lane, so a specific lane must be selected to observe its individual value  
ROCm Profiling on the RDNA Architecture

- Objective 1   
  - Explain how AMD ROCm profiling tools analyze GPU execution on RDNA architectures using trace-based methodologies.   
- Objective 2  
  - Distinguish GPU profiling (ROCProfiler-SDK/rocprofv3) from system profiling (ROCm System Profiler)  
- ROCm Profiling on the RDNA Architecture  
  - Identifies kernel-level and system-level bottlenecks   
  - Analyzes kernel execution, memory behaviour and runtime overheads  
  - Provides visibility into CPU-GPU interactions and synchronication costs.   
  - Combines trace timelines with kernel timings summaries for optimization   
  - Supports iterative tuning of GPU applications for better efficiency.   
- RDNA GPU execution involves asynchronous CPU-GPU interaction.   
  - Performance depends on efficient kernel dispatch and scheduling   
  - Memory transfers and synchronication operations introduce overheads   
  - Trace based Profiling   
    - Exposes idly gaps, delays and pipeline stalls on execution timelines.   
    - Helps improve concurrency across streams and execution queues.   
    - Identifies GPU-compute vs API overhead / memory latency bound regions.   
    - CUDA profiling provides extensive hardware counters \- RDNA profiling relies more on trace based timelines.   
- ROCm Profiling Tooling \- Overview   
  - ROCm Profiling Ecosystem has 2 tools  
    - ROCProfiler-SDK (rocprofv3)  
      - GPU tracing and profiling framework   
      - Outputs:   
        - Perfetto traces   
        - CSV/JSON summaries   
        - ROCPD SQLite databases.   
    - ROCm System Profiler   
      - CPU and system level performance analysis  
      - Ouptut:   
        - Perfetto traces  
        - JSON data.   
  - Visualization with Perfetto  
- What RDNA Profiling Supports   
  - Profiling on RDNA architecture focuses on trace-based observation of execution across multiple layers.   
  - GPU Kernel Dispatch Tracing with precise execution timing.   
  - Runtime API Tracing for application level behaviour.   
  - Memory Transfer Tracing \- Host device communication & intra-GPU transfers.   
- Execution visualized through Perfetto- compatible timeline.   
- Support for system level CPU sampling and instrumentation   
- GPU traces captured with rocprofv3 and CPU traces with ROCm System Profiler.   
- RDNA Profiling considerations   
  - Architectural Constraints   
    - Hardware counters may be limited or unavailable on RDNA GPUs, trace timelines prioritized.   
  - Profiling Implications: Primarily trace-based analysis rather than microarchitectural metrics.   
  - COmplexity and Workflow: Some analyses may require multi-pass or specialized profiling workflows.   
    - Asynchronous execution can complicate the timeline interpretation.   
  - Effective profiling requires combining multiple tools and carefully analyzing execution behaviour.   
- ROCProfiler SDK (rocprofv3) \- Overview  
  - AMD unified GPU profiling and tracing framework  
- 

| Recorded Data  | API calls  | Kernel diispatch | Memory operations |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Supported Hardware | Designed for ROCm platform compatible GPUs, including RDNA architectures |  |  |
| Export Formats  | Perfetto for visualization, CSV and JSON for summaries, ROCPD SQLite for structured analysis |  |  |
| Configuration | YAML based configuration for reproducible, repeatable profiling workflows.  |  |  |

Tracing Types: Runtime vs Kernel 

- Tracing has 2 types:   
  - Runtime tracking: has the CPU thread \-\> API calls \-\> Memory operations \-\> Sync Captures CPU-side overhead and inefficient API usage patterns.   
  - Kernel tracing: GPU Kernel A Kernel B. Captures kernel duration frequency and scheduling.   
    - Combines HIP \+ HSA \+ kerel activity into unified execution timelines.   
  - Runtime tracing captures CPU side overhead and inefficient usage patterns.   
  - Kernel Tracing: Captures the kernel duration, frequency and scheduling.   
- Kernel Hotspot Analysis   
  - Identifies kernels that consuming the highest total execution time \-\> Compares   
  - Compares average vs peak execution durations.  
  - Evaluates kernel launch frequence and workload distribution   
  - Derives hotspot data from rocprofv3 outputs.   
  - Focuses optimization on the most time-consuming kernels.   
  - Enables iterative and data-driven GPU optimization.   
- Profetto Timeline Visualization (ROCm Trace Analysis)  
  - Primary visualization layer for ROCm profiling outputs enabling sequence of API calls HSA runtime activity and unified view  
  - Highlights execution delays idle gaps and overlaps.  
  - Offers filtering and zooming for detailed inspection of specific events, making it essential for understanding end to end application behaviour.  
- Rocprofv3   
  - Used when detailed analysis of GPU kernel execution behaviour in detail is required.   
  - Inspect HIP and HSA runtime activity sequences.   
  - Detect API overhead and other inefficiencies.   
  - Identify kernel hotspots and optimization opportunities.   
  - Visualize GPU execution timelines uing Perfetto   
  - Study asynchronous execution and dependencies.   
  - Perform iterative GPU performance optimization.   
- ROCm Systems Profiler   
  - Captures system wide CPU and GPU activity for performance analysis   
  - Recorded data \- CPU call stacks, thread behaviour, runtime events, OS level interactions, SYnchronization behaviour.   
  - Export formats \- Perfetto for timeline visualization.   
    - JSON metadata for structured analysis. 	  
  - Benefits \- Reveals CPU bottlenecks and runtime inefficiencies that affect GPU execution.   
- Profiling Modes   
  - Sampling Mode: Collects periodic CPU call stacks with low overhead to identify time-consuming functions.   
  - Instrumentation Mode: Measures function entry/exit timings   
    - Provides inclusive and exclusive function cost breakdowns.   
  - Binary Rewrite Mode: Enables persistent instrumentation for reproducible and large scale profiling workflows.   
    - Instrumenting means adding extra code (probes) to a program so it records its own activity, such as when functions start and end and how long they take. Binary rewrite mode patches these profiling hooks into a copy of your executable once, so you can run that same instrumented file repeatedly (including across many nodes) and get consistent, comparable results without re-instrumenting every run.  
  - Together they give flexibility for analyzing CPU side performance.   
- CPU-GPU Interaction Analysis.   
  - CPU thread activity combined with GPU execution timelines.   
  - Tells CPU delays affect kernel dispatch timing.   
  - This helps identify blocking calls and synchronization points.   
  - Along with concurrency patterns and idle GPU periods highlighted.   
- Result: Developers can improve overlap between CPU and GPU.   
- Recommended RDNA Profiling Strategy   
  - Start with runtime tracing (rocprofv3) for a baseline understanding   
  - Identify kernel hotspots that contribute most to execution time   
  - Use timeline analysis to understand execution flow behaviour  
  - Analyze CPU behaviour with ROCm Systems Profiler.   
  - Investigate deeper issues using instrumentation when needed.   
  - Combine GPU and CPU analysis to optimize the full execution pipeline.   
  - Follow an iterative profiling \-\> analysis \-\> optimization loop.   
- Summary   
  - RDNA architecture profiling relies primarily on trace timelines and kernel timing summaries, as hardware counter availability is limited compared to HPC class GPUs.   
  - Rocprofv3 and ROCm Systems Profiler provide comlementatry views of performance, enabling analysis of GPU execution adn CPU-GPU interaction.   
  - Perfetto serves as the unified visualization layer, allowing correlation of runtime activity, kernel execution nd system behaviour for effective optimization.
